holding_summary: The court held that furniture supplied under a conditional-sale/bailment agreement to a boarding-house keeper for use in furnishing her boarding house was liable to the landlord's distress for rent, distinguishing it from the personal property of an actual boarder, which longstanding precedent exempts as goods necessarily on the premises in the way of trade.

quotes.text: In Riddle v. Welden, 5 Wh. 9, the goods of a boarder were held not to be liable for rent due by the keeper of the boarding house.

holding_summary: The Superior Court affirmed a verdict for a hotel guest whose jewelry was stolen from his room, holding that under the Act of 1855 an innkeeper is practically an insurer of the kind of valuables a guest commonly and prudently keeps in his room, and that the guest's overnight absence from the room did not constitute negligence as a matter of law barring recovery. The court declined to reach the guest-versus-boarder distinction argued by the appellants because it had not been raised at trial.

quotes.text: This leaves the innkeeper, as to the articles described (unless stolen by the servant or companion of the guest), practically in the position of an insurer, under the rule of the common law as laid down in Shultz v. Wall, 134 Pa. 262, Walsh v. Porterfield, 87 Pa. 376, and Houser v. Tully, 62 Pa. 92.

holding_summary: The Superior Court affirmed judgment for a landlady who had leased her boarding house and furniture to a tenant for a year, holding the lease properly admitted in evidence despite her coverture, that the tenant could not dispute the lessor's title because she took possession under it without eviction by any paramount title, and that the lessor's occasional bad language toward other boarders while herself boarding in the house did not as a matter of law amount to an eviction excusing the rent.

quotes.text: On January 9, 1896, she entered into a written agreement with Ida M. Hobensack, leasing the house and furniture to the latter for one year, from January 15, 1896, at the annual rent of $900, payable in monthly instalments of $75.00, on the 15th of each month in advance, together with rooms and first class boarding for the plaintiff and her daughter.
This case falls within the general principle which forbids a tenant to impeach his landlord's title: Howard v. Murphy, 23 Pa. 173.

Under the terms of the lease the lessor had a right to remain in the house as a hoarder; this right, however, was subject to the implied condition that it must be exercised in a reasonable and orderly manner.

holding_summary: The Supreme Court held that a married woman who leased and paid for boarding-house property with her own separate funds, furnished it herself, and personally managed the boarders was entitled to keep the profits of that business as her own separate estate, free from seizure by her husband's creditors.
